note: Token ceilings projected by the dry run, never measured. Live runs record what they actually spent on their result files in evals/results/. Pass a cap to the runner with --budget-tokens; nothing here is read automatically. The model id in `source` does not change these figures: a dry run counts prompt tokens with count_tokens and reports each call's requested max_tokens, neither of which depends on which model was asked for. tests/test_budget_is_current.py re-runs the projection and fails if any number here has drifted, which is how this file went a day stale before.
why_the_default_is_low: Deliberately below the projected ceiling of six of the eighteen examples. A cap that stops a run is a partial result you can raise and resume from cache; a cap that never bites is not a budget. Start here, read the partial, raise it for the example you actually want.
how_these_were_set: Each is the example's dry-run ceiling rounded up with headroom, except order_zero (calls no model at all) and routing (see routing_is_underprojected). The whole set at these caps is about 4.7M tokens, well above the 3.0M ceiling, so a cap only bites when something has gone wrong.
routing_is_underprojected: routing's dry number, 5,410, is not a ceiling. Its control flow parses one classification word from the model, and the dry-run stand-in's placeholder text is not a label it recognizes, so the projection always follows the cheapest branch: the fallback, which calls no model again at all. A real run sends most questions down the lookup branch, which retrieves and calls the model a second time with the sources in the prompt. Its cap here is set from rag's ceiling instead, which is the shape that branch actually takes. See docs/EVALS.md, 'Dry run'.
context_engineering_is_the_expensive_one: It puts the whole document set in every prompt by design, which is the point of the page: 835,880 input tokens over 60 questions, about 14,000 a question, against rag's 519. Run it last, and only once, unless you are measuring exactly that.
the_grader_is_not_in_these_numbers: Every figure in this file projects the answering model only. 28 of the 60 questions are rubric-graded, and each one that reaches the grader is a second model call the dry run cannot project, because its prompt contains the answer the model has not given yet. Its output is bounded: the runner asks the grader for at most 10 tokens, so at most 280 output tokens an example. Its input is the question, the checklist and the answer, so budget for roughly the size of one answer per rubric question on top of the ceiling below. A real run now records what it actually cost as grader_calls, grader_tokens_in and grader_tokens_out on the result file; read those after the first example and you will know the real multiplier for the rest.
what_a_cap_does: The runner adds one question's tokens, then compares against the cap, so it can overshoot by at most a single question before it stops. It writes a result file marked "partial": true with questions_run below questions_total. Responses are cached by (model id, prompt hash), so raising the cap and re-running pays only for what the first run did not reach.
dollars: Deliberately absent. A per-token price belongs to one model and changes without notice, and a number written here would go stale silently and read as this site's own claim about a maker's price. Multiply the token figures by the price on the maker's own page on the day you run, and put that price in the price table you hand examples/ops.
